vpc.title: VPC
vpc.body: A Virtual Private Cloud is your own fenced-off region of the AWS network. Nothing gets in or out unless you build a way. Inside it, subnets divide the space; each subnet sits in one Availability Zone.
simplifications: The game has one VPC with fixed subnets. Real VPCs can be laid out any way you like.

internet-gateway.title: Internet Gateway
internet-gateway.body: The gate between your VPC and the internet. Attaching one is not enough on its own: a subnet only becomes public when its route table sends internet traffic (0.0.0.0/0) to the gateway.

route-table.title: Route table
route-table.body: A list of signposts for traffic leaving a subnet. Every route table has a local route for the VPC that cannot be removed. When several routes match, the most specific one wins.
simplifications: Destinations are named choices (Internet, S3, DynamoDB) rather than address ranges you type.

load-balancer.title: Application Load Balancer
load-balancer.body: The front door. It receives web requests and shares them between healthy targets, across Availability Zones. An internet-facing load balancer lives in public subnets in at least two zones.
simplifications: Targets always receive traffic on HTTP 80; the load balancer handles HTTPS (certificates are assumed).
One listener and one set of targets. Real load balancers can have several, with rules.
Health is judged instantly, and when an Availability Zone fails, the load balancer stops sending kites there the same minute. Real health checks take a few intervals to change their mind.
The load balancer itself never runs out of capacity. Real ones scale automatically, but a sudden spike can briefly outpace them.

security-group.title: Security group
security-group.body: A firewall worn by a resource: the pencilled outline around a cloud. It holds allow rules only; anything not allowed is refused. It is stateful: the reply to an allowed request is always let through. A rule's source can be another security group, meaning "anything wearing that group".
simplifications: Ports are picked from a short list of named choices.

network-acl.title: Network ACL
network-acl.body: A fence on a subnet's boundary. Rules are numbered and read lowest first; the first match decides, and it can allow or deny, so a deny must be numbered before the allow it is an exception to. It is stateless: a reply needs its own rule, usually for ephemeral ports 1024–65535. The VPC's default ACL allows everything; a new custom ACL denies everything until you add rules. Leave room between rule numbers (100, 110, 120) so a rule can be added between two others later without renumbering.
simplifications: Sources are "anywhere" or one of a few named address ranges.
Replies are checked against one representative ephemeral port.
There is no limit on rules per ACL (AWS allows 20 each way unless you ask for more).

ec2-instance.title: EC2 instance
ec2-instance.body: A virtual server. It lives in exactly one subnet, wears security groups, and can be given an IAM role so the software on it can call other AWS services without any stored keys.
simplifications: Instances in the game never have public addresses, so nothing on the ground can reach them directly.
Machine images and instance families are left out.

nat-gateway.title: NAT Gateway
nat-gateway.body: A one-way door. It sits in a public subnet and lets resources in private subnets start connections out to the internet. It never lets the internet start a connection in. It lives in one Availability Zone, and it is charged by the hour and by the gigabyte.

s3-bucket.title: S3 bucket
s3-bucket.body: Object storage, outside your VPC, holding as much as you care to put in it. Block Public Access is on by default and overrides any policy that would open the bucket to everyone. Every new object is encrypted at rest: by default with SSE-S3 (keys S3 manages), or with SSE-KMS and a KMS key, AWS managed (aws/s3) or your own. Changing the default encryption affects new objects only.
simplifications: Block Public Access is one switch here; in AWS it is four related settings.
Bucket policies can grant to everyone or to a named role, nothing finer.

The objects a red Cloudling reads are the ones stored before the level began, encrypted with SSE-S3. The application's own reads and writes are of objects under the bucket's current default encryption.
No S3 Bucket Keys, object-level encryption headers or DSSE-KMS.

iam-role.title: IAM role
iam-role.body: A set of permissions that a resource can wear. IAM denies everything by default; a statement must explicitly allow an action, and an explicit deny beats any allow. Grant only what is used: that is least privilege.
simplifications: Permissions are grouped into families such as s3:Read, s3:Write and kms:Use, on one resource or on everything (*).
There are no users or access keys in the game: only roles.

concept-public-subnet.title: What makes a subnet public?
concept-public-subnet.body: One thing only: its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an Internet Gateway attached to the VPC. Not its name, not its position. And even then, a security group must allow each connection in.

concept-security-group-chaining.title: Chaining security groups
concept-security-group-chaining.body: Instead of allowing an address range, a rule can name another security group. "Allow HTTP from the load balancer's group" stays correct however many load balancer nodes there are and whatever their addresses. Each tier trusts only the tier in front of it.

concept-roles-not-keys.title: Roles, not keys
concept-roles-not-keys.body: Software on an instance gets its permissions from the instance's IAM role: short-lived credentials that AWS hands out and rotates. Nothing secret is stored on the server. Without a role, the instance cannot sign a request at all.

gateway-endpoint.title: Gateway endpoint
gateway-endpoint.body: A private road from your VPC to S3 or DynamoDB. It is not a thing you place in a subnet: it appears as a route in the route table, with a prefix list (the service's address ranges) as the destination. Because that route is more specific than 0.0.0.0/0, traffic for the service takes it and never leaves the AWS network. Gateway endpoints exist for S3 and DynamoDB only, and have no additional charge.
simplifications: Endpoint policies, which can restrict what the endpoint may be used for, are left out.
In AWS you create the endpoint and choose route tables for it; here you add the route directly.

concept-cost.title: Paying for what you leave running
concept-cost.body: Some resources cost money for every hour they exist, whether or not anything uses them. A NAT Gateway is one: it is charged by the hour and by the gigabyte. A gateway endpoint to S3 costs nothing. Choosing the cheaper path that still does the job is part of building well.
simplifications: Coins are illustrative units for comparing choices. They are not real AWS prices.

auto-scaling-group.title: Auto Scaling group
auto-scaling-group.body: A fleet of identical EC2 instances with a minimum, a maximum and a desired size. It spreads its instances across the subnets you choose, and so across Availability Zones. With a scaling policy it changes its own size: a target tracking policy keeps a measure such as average CPU near a target, launching instances when the fleet is busy and removing them when it is quiet. Attached to a load balancer, its instances register as targets automatically.
simplifications: Each Cloudling keeps one kite up, and every instance has room for a fixed number of kites by size (5, 10 or 20). A new instance takes 2 minutes to start serving. Real launch times and capacities vary.
Only target tracking on CPU is offered. Step, simple, scheduled and predictive scaling are left out.

When CPU has stayed below the target for 2 minutes, the group removes enough instances to bring it back up to the target, but never more than half the fleet at once. AWS also scales in more gradually than out, at a pace it decides itself.
A kite that finds every target busy times out in the same tick. Real requests wait in a queue first, and some are served late.
Every kite in a crowd is treated alike, so one journey through each instance stands for all the kites that instance is sent.
A group keeps at least one instance; AWS allows a minimum of zero.

Launch templates and instance warm-up settings are left out. Instances are replaced only when their Availability Zone fails; real groups also replace instances that fail their health checks for other reasons.
A group can have at most 16 instances here, so the sky can draw every one. Real groups can be far larger.

When an Availability Zone fails, the group notices its instances there are unhealthy 2 minutes later, terminates them and launches replacements in its other zones, which serve 2 minutes after that. Real health checks and launches vary.

cloudwatch.title: CloudWatch
cloudwatch.body: The weather station. CloudWatch collects metrics, such as the CPU use of a fleet or the number of requests at a load balancer, and alarms watch a metric against a threshold. An alarm is either OK or in ALARM, and can trigger an action such as scaling a group. With a target tracking policy, EC2 Auto Scaling creates and manages the alarms for you.
simplifications: Metrics are measured once a minute, and an alarm acts on a single reading: above the target at once, below it after 2 minutes. Real alarms wait for several readings, and the scale-in alarm waits much longer.
CPU is modelled as the share of the targets' room in use: kites ÷ room.

cloudtrail.title: CloudTrail
cloudtrail.body: CloudTrail records the calls made to AWS in your account: who called which action, on what, from where and when. It is on in every account with nothing to set up, and its Event history keeps the last 90 days of management events, free. Every call to KMS is one of them, so each use of a KMS key is recorded, with the role behind it: storing an object (GenerateDataKey) or reading one (Decrypt).
points: Management events are recorded by default: creating a bucket, changing a security group, every call to KMS. Data events, such as reading or writing an object in S3, are not: you add them to a trail, at extra cost.
For a record longer than 90 days, create a trail: it delivers the events to an S3 bucket.
With SSE-S3, S3 manages the keys itself and never calls KMS, so CloudTrail has no record of key use. With SSE-KMS there is a record of every call, whether the key is an AWS managed key or your own.
Each Session Manager session start is a StartSession call, recorded with the identity that started it. An SSH login with a shared key leaves no record in AWS at all.
CloudTrail and CloudWatch are different services: CloudTrail records who did what through the AWS API, and CloudWatch measures how things are running.
simplifications: CloudTrail is not drawn in the sky and its records are not shown: it is on in every account, so there is nothing to place.
S3 Bucket Keys, which reuse a bucket-level key for a while and so make far fewer KMS calls (and fewer records), are left out.

concept-elasticity.title: Elasticity
concept-elasticity.body: Matching capacity to demand as demand changes: more when it is busy, less when it is quiet, without anyone doing it by hand. It is one of the main reasons to build in the cloud. The alternative is to buy for the busiest day and pay for that capacity on every other day.

concept-cidr.title: What does /16 mean?
concept-cidr.body: An address range is written as a starting address and a number after the slash, called CIDR notation. An IPv4 address has 32 bits; the number says how many of them are fixed. The rest are free to vary, so a smaller number means a bigger range, and each step down doubles it.
points: /16: 65,536 addresses. 10.0.0.0/16 runs from 10.0.0.0 to 10.0.255.255. This is the largest range AWS allows for a VPC, and the size of this one.
/24: 256 addresses, e.g. 10.0.1.0 to 10.0.1.255. Each subnet here is a /24 carved out of the VPC's range. AWS keeps the first four and the last address of every subnet, so 251 are yours.
/28: 16 addresses. The smallest range AWS allows for a VPC or a subnet.
/32: exactly one address. Too small for a subnet; used in rules to name a single machine, e.g. 203.0.113.10/32.
/0: every address. 0.0.0.0/0 is the "Internet" or "Anywhere" in routes and rules.
A subnet's range must sit inside its VPC's range, and subnets in one VPC must not overlap.
simplifications: The game never asks you to work out ranges: the VPC and subnets come ready-made, and IPv6 is left out.

concept-listener.title: Listener
concept-listener.body: A listener is the load balancer's ear. It waits for connections on one protocol and port, such as HTTPS 443, and passes the requests it hears on to the targets. The security group must allow the same port, or a request never reaches the listener.
points: HTTPS 443 encrypts the conversation between the Cloudling and the load balancer. HTTP 80 sends it in the clear, where anyone on the way could read it.

In real life, an HTTPS listener needs an SSL/TLS certificate deployed on the load balancer. The certificate proves the website is really yours. AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) can issue one and renew it for you.
The load balancer decrypts each request and sends it on to its targets. Here the targets always receive HTTP 80, inside the VPC.
simplifications: Certificates are assumed: the game never asks you to request or attach one.
One listener per load balancer, with no listener rules.

concept-bastion-host.title: Bastion host
concept-bastion-host.body: A bastion host, or jump box, is the traditional way for people to reach EC2 instances that have no public address. It is a small EC2 instance in a public subnet. An administrator connects to it first, usually with SSH on port 22, and from there connects on to the EC2 instance in the private subnet.
points: The bastion's security group allows SSH only from known addresses, such as an office's range, never from Anywhere.
The private EC2 instances allow SSH only from the bastion's security group: the same chaining as the load balancer and the application servers.
Each hop needs credentials, usually an SSH key pair. An attacker would need the bastion's address and those keys; the red Cloudling has neither.
A bastion is a target in its own right, so it has to be patched, watched and kept small.
AWS also offers a way to do without one: Systems Manager Session Manager needs no open inbound ports, no bastion host and no SSH keys. Access is controlled with IAM, and sessions can be logged.
simplifications: Level 9's bastion host runs only SSH, and its SSH key pair is assumed rather than modelled. The red Cloudling never has the key; in AWS a leaked key is the real danger.

rds-database.title: RDS database
rds-database.body: Amazon RDS runs a relational database (MySQL, PostgreSQL and others) for you: AWS installs it, patches it and backs it up. It lives in private subnets, and only the application tier talks to it, on the engine's port.
points: It needs a DB subnet group: private subnets in at least two Availability Zones, even when the database runs in one. That is what lets it become Multi-AZ later.

Its security group should allow MySQL 3306 (or PostgreSQL 5432) from the application tier's security group, not from an address range. An address range belongs to one subnet, in one zone; a security group follows the instances wherever they run.
Single-AZ: one copy, in one zone. If that zone fails, the database is down until the zone comes back.

Multi-AZ: RDS keeps a standby in another zone, updated with every write as it happens. If the primary's zone fails, RDS fails over to the standby by itself, typically in 60–120 seconds. The database's endpoint (its address) moves with it, so the application reconnects to the same name.
The standby serves nothing until it takes over: it is not for spreading reads. Read replicas are the feature for that.

Encryption at rest is chosen when a database is created, with the AWS managed key aws/rds or a customer managed key, and cannot be switched on later. To encrypt an existing database, snapshot it, copy the snapshot with encryption on, restore a new database from the copy, and point the application at it. The application needs no KMS permission: RDS uses the key itself.
simplifications: Database users and passwords, engine versions, storage and backups are left out: the application always has the right credentials here.
A failover takes exactly 2 minutes here. In AWS it is typically 60–120 seconds, and can take longer.
After a failover the database has no standby until its old zone recovers, and zones do not recover during a run here.

Replacing a database with an encrypted copy happens at once here, keeping its name. In AWS the copy and restore take a while, writes must pause or be replicated meanwhile, and keeping the old name means renaming the old database first.

concept-static-stability.title: Surviving the loss of an Availability Zone
concept-static-stability.body: Each AWS Region has several Availability Zones: separate data centres with their own power, cooling and networking, close enough to each other for fast links. A zone can fail. An application rides it out if nothing it needs lives in only one zone, and the zones that are left can carry the load.
points: Spread the compute: an Auto Scaling group across subnets in two zones. When one zone fails, the load balancer stops sending it requests, and the group launches replacements in the zone that is up.
Keep the data available: a Multi-AZ database fails over to its standby in the other zone.
Chain security groups by name, not by address. An address range is one subnet's, in one zone; when the instances move, the rule does not.
Static stability: run enough in each zone to carry the load on its own. Then nothing has to launch in a hurry when a zone fails. Replacements take minutes, and the visitors do not wait.
simplifications: Here a zone fails all at once and stays down until the end of the run. Real outages are often partial and end; when a zone recovers, Auto Scaling spreads the group across the zones again.

waf-web-acl.title: AWS WAF web ACL
waf-web-acl.body: A web application firewall in front of the load balancer. A web ACL reads each request the load balancer accepts and blocks it, or lets it on, before a target is chosen. Its rules can block address ranges (IP sets), an address sending too many requests (rate-based rules) and attacks carried in the request (AWS managed rules such as the Core rule set, which covers cross-site scripting and file inclusion). A blocked request gets 403 Forbidden. Security groups and network ACLs see only addresses and ports; WAF sees what a request carries. In the newer AWS console a web ACL is called a protection pack.
simplifications: Rules run in a fixed order: IP set, rate-based rule, then the Core rule set. In AWS you set each rule's priority.

A flood's rate is given for each Cloudling, and once it is over the limit every request it sends is blocked. A real rate-based rule checks about every 10 seconds and blocks only the requests over the limit, while the rate lasts.
Every malicious payload in the game is one the Core rule set recognises. SQL injection needs AWS's separate SQL database rule group.
No logging, Bot Control, CAPTCHA or custom responses.

concept-defence-in-depth.title: Security at every layer
concept-defence-in-depth.body: One of the Well-Architected security principles: apply security at all layers, because no single control sees everything. A network ACL turns addresses away at a subnet's edge, a security group decides which ports a cloud accepts and from whom, and AWS WAF reads the requests themselves. Each stops what the others cannot: here, the block-listed range at the edge, and the hidden script and the flood in WAF.

kms-key.title: KMS key
kms-key.body: AWS Key Management Service keeps encryption keys and uses them for you: the keys never leave it. S3, RDS and many other services ask KMS to use a key whenever they encrypt or decrypt your data. An AWS managed key (aws/s3, aws/rds) is created and controlled by AWS for one service. A customer managed key is yours: you decide who may use it, you can switch on yearly rotation, and every use is recorded in CloudTrail. It costs about a dollar a month.
points: Who may use a key is decided by its key policy. The default key policy lets IAM policies in the account decide, so a role needs permission to use the key.

With SSE-KMS and a customer managed key, S3 calls KMS on the caller's behalf, and KMS checks the caller's permissions: storing an object needs kms:GenerateDataKey, reading one needs kms:Decrypt. Without them, the request fails at the key, even when the role may use the bucket.
Keys are Regional: a key protects data in its own Region, and its key policy applies only there.
simplifications: kms:Use stands for the permissions S3 needs from a caller: kms:GenerateDataKey to store an object and kms:Decrypt to read one.
Every key here has the default key policy, which leaves permissions to IAM. Key policies, grants, aliases, rotation and multi-Region keys are left out.
A key that still encrypts something cannot be removed. In AWS you schedule a key's deletion, 7 to 30 days ahead, and data under a deleted key can never be read again.

session-manager.title: Session Manager
session-manager.body: AWS Systems Manager Session Manager gives you a shell on an instance with no inbound port open, no public address, no bastion host and no SSH key. The SSM Agent on the instance connects out to Systems Manager over HTTPS 443 and keeps that connection open; a session runs over it. Who may start a session is decided by IAM, and every session start is recorded in CloudTrail.
points: An instance is managed once its agent has registered with Systems Manager, using the instance's IAM role: the role needs the permissions in the AWS managed policy AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore.
The agent needs HTTPS (443) out to the Systems Manager endpoints: from a private subnet, through a NAT Gateway or through interface VPC endpoints.
The person starting a session needs permission too (ssm:StartSession), and signs in with their own AWS identity: nothing depends on where they are connecting from.
What happens inside a session can be logged to S3 or CloudWatch Logs, once you switch that on.
simplifications: ssm:ManagedInstance stands for the permissions in AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore, and names Session Manager; the managed policy grants them on every resource (*).
Placing Session Manager stands for choosing to use it: in AWS it is always there in a Region. The SSM Agent is assumed to be installed, as it is on Amazon Linux.
The operator's own permission to start a session (ssm:StartSession) is assumed.
Interface VPC endpoints are left out: "Session Manager in the real world" says what they need.

session-manager-real-world.title: Session Manager in the real world
session-manager-real-world.body: In this level Session Manager needs three things: Session Manager itself, a role that lets the instance's agent register, and a way out on HTTPS 443. A real account needs a few details more, and most surprises come from them. Nothing on this card is something you have to set up in the game.
points: The SSM Agent: preinstalled on Amazon Linux 2, Amazon Linux 2023 and many other AWS images; on others you install it.
An instance profile: the EC2 instance's role, with the AWS managed policy AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore attached.
HTTPS (443) out to three endpoints in the Region: ssm, ssmmessages and ec2messages. Network ACLs are stateless, so their replies need allowing too, on ephemeral ports.
From a private subnet, either a NAT Gateway, as in this level, or interface VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) for those three services, with no internet access at all.

With interface endpoints: switch on private DNS for each endpoint, switch on the VPC's DNS hostnames and DNS resolution settings, and let the endpoints' security group allow HTTPS in from the instances. Missing any of these is the classic reason a private instance never shows up as managed.
The person starting a session needs ssm:StartSession and, from the command line, the Session Manager plugin for the AWS CLI.

concept-encryption-at-rest.title: Encryption at rest
concept-encryption-at-rest.body: Stored data is kept encrypted, so whoever got hold of the disks or the backups would find only scrambled bytes. It does not decide who may read the data: whoever the bucket or the database lets in gets it decrypted, which is why closing the bucket mattered first. Access control and encryption are different defences. S3 encrypts every new object by default, DynamoDB always encrypts, and an RDS database is encrypted if it was created that way. A customer managed key adds a second permission, checked separately: using the key.
